source: METR RCT: Becker et al. (2025) Early-2025 AI and experienced open-source developer productivity
finding: Randomised trial inside real repositories. Developers with AI allowed took longer, not shorter. Both developers and experts predicted a speedup.
numbers: 16 experienced open-source developers, 246 tasks (about 2.0 h each), paid $150/h. Forecast before: AI cuts time 24%. Estimate after: AI cut time 20%. Measured: AI raised completion time 19%. Raw difference was 34% but AI-allowed issues were slightly harder after randomisation.
limits: Own long-run repositories, moderate AI experience (mostly Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet). Early-2025 tools.
agent_relevance: Self-report of speed is a poor measurement tool. Our agent evaluations need an objective outcome, not the agent's or user's felt gain.

source: METR RCT: screen-recording sub-study
finding: Researchers labelled screen recordings to check protocol compliance and to see where time went. AI use was real in most AI-allowed tasks, and some rule-breaking was found in AI-disallowed ones.
numbers: 143 h of video labelled (29% of hours, 128 recordings); 74 recordings (84 h) usable after filtering. Developers did not use AI in only 16.4% of 44 valid AI-allowed recordings. 3 of 54 AI-disallowed recordings showed AI use (about 6% cheating). Using total screen-recording time instead of self-reported time gave a 25% slowdown.
limits: Labelling is slow, so only a subset was coded. Cheating rate is from a small sample.
agent_relevance: Observation by recording beats self-report as a check on process. Log the agent's full trace and audit compliance with the assigned condition.

source: METR RCT: experience with the tool as moderator
finding: Slowdown did not clearly shrink with Cursor experience up to 50 hours. Authors say a high skill ceiling is plausible.
numbers: Up to 50 hours of Cursor experience, no clear improvement in speedup. Few developers had more than 50 hours. Developers wrote about 47% more code per hour of AI-allowed time (p = 0.16, not significant).
limits: Few data points beyond 50 hours. Several developers mis-reported prior Cursor hours.
agent_relevance: Training and skill with the tool is a moderator that single trials cannot resolve. Report tool-experience in agent-vs-human studies.

source: Peng et al. (2023) The impact of AI on developer productivity: evidence from GitHub Copilot
finding: Controlled trial with freelance programmers on one task. Copilot group finished much faster. Gains were larger for less experienced developers.
numbers: 95 professional programmers from Upwork (166 offers sent, 95 accepted). Task: write an HTTP server in JavaScript, 12 tests. Treated group 55.8% faster (95% CI 21 to 89%). Treated success rate was about 7 points higher (not clearly significant). Less experienced, older (25-44) and heavy daily coders gained more.
limits: One small greenfield task, wide confidence interval, freelancers, volunteers. Contrasts with the METR result: small isolated task vs large mature codebase.
agent_relevance: Effect sign flips with task type and codebase familiarity. Do not generalise a benchmark-style gain to real-repo work.

source: Cui et al. (2025) Effects of generative AI on high-skilled work: three field experiments
finding: Three company-run randomised field trials of a coding assistant. Pooled estimate showed more completed tasks, but each trial was noisy.
numbers: 4,867 developers at Microsoft, Accenture and a Fortune 100 firm. Pooled IV estimate: +26.08% weekly pull requests (SE 10.3%), +13.55% commits (SE 10.0%), +38.38% builds (SE 12.55%). At Microsoft only the pull-request effect was significant. Share of treated developers with positive adoption: 37.09% Microsoft, 12.90% Accenture, 34.01% Fortune 100 (figure panel labels). Junior developers gained more.
limits: Ad hoc business experiments, post-registered (AEARCTR-0014530). Low take-up, large variance. Output counts, not quality. Build success rate was negative at Accenture.
agent_relevance: Intention-to-treat vs treatment-on-treated matters. For agent trials, report adoption and compliance, not just assignment.

source: Cui et al. (2025): pooled estimate versus single-site estimates
finding: The single-site results are individually weak. Only pooling across three experiments gives a clear signal. Shows why one small trial is not enough.
numbers: Microsoft: only pull requests significant at usual levels. Accenture and Fortune 100: same direction but often not significant. Authors note the exact implementation was ad hoc because trials served business decisions.
limits: Pooling weights periods by treatment difference, which is an analysis choice.
agent_relevance: Pool across tasks and repos before claiming an agent effect. Expect wide intervals.

source: Salman, Tosun Misirli, Juristo (2015) Are students representatives of professionals in SE experiments?
finding: Compared a student TDD experiment with a professional TDD experiment on code-quality metrics. Groups differ when applying the familiar method, and are similar when both use a new method.
numbers: 17 graduate students (Madrid) vs 24 professionals (Helsinki, Oulu, Kuala Lumpur). Code-quality metrics differed in 55% and 49% of values for the test-last (TLD) and first TDD treatments. 100 hypotheses on TDD1 showed no major differences; on TDD2, differences in 53% of cases. Conclusion: neither group better when applying a new technology.
limits: Two experiments differed in design, protocol and number of tasks (professionals did one task, students four). Source opened is a course slide deck of the paper, not the full ICSE text.
agent_relevance: Novelty of the method equalises groups. A new scaffold for an agent is also new to any human baseline, so novice-vs-expert comparisons need care.

source: Romano, Sferratore, Scanniello (2025) Professionals vs students on bug fixing
finding: Students beat professionals on a bug-fixing task, which goes against much earlier evidence. Likely moderators are setting stress, seniority and degree.
numbers: 62 bachelor students vs 42 professionals from two multinational companies (three offices). Students fixed 3.315 bugs per hour on average (median 3) vs 2.254 (median 2.667). Mann-Whitney p < 0.001, Cliff's delta 0.471 (medium) on one metric and 0.368 (medium) on the other. Against two of three professional sites the effect was large (delta 0.606 and 0.565; 0.542 and 0.483), Bonferroni-adjusted p 0.001 to 0.008. No difference against the third site (p = 0.33, adjusted 0.991).
limits: Settings differed on purpose: professionals had interruptions and stress, were older with more master's degrees. Short paper, authors draw no firm conclusion.
agent_relevance: Human baselines are fragile to setting. When we compare an agent with humans, state who the humans were and what conditions they worked under.

source: Related work in Romano et al. (2025): earlier student vs professional comparisons
finding: Earlier work mostly found small differences between trained students and professionals. Differences appear when students are freshmen or the task is familiar to professionals.
numbers: Host et al.: only minor differences between project managers and graduate students on effort and lead-time judgements. Counsell: no substantial difference in class cohesion ratings. Runeson: freshmen differ from graduates; data too thin to say graduates match professionals.
limits: Secondary summary of those studies, not the originals.
agent_relevance: Rule of thumb: trained students are a fair proxy for novel methods, not for expert-practice effects.

source: Santos et al. (2020) Increasing validity through replication: an illustrative TDD case
finding: Three TDD experiments (baseline plus two replications) gave inconsistent results, which the authors trace to moderators. The effect was never statistically significant.
numbers: Test-driven vs iterative test-last on four tasks. TDD vs ITL difference not significant in any replication. On the BSK task direction was ITL>TDD in the baseline but ITL<TDD in both replications. In RE2, MF and SDK favoured ITL and BSK and MR favoured TDD. Task effect sizes ranged from medium to large but all 95% CIs crossed 0.
limits: Small samples. Candidate moderators: operationalisation of the response variable, allocation of subjects to treatments, working outside the lab, provision of stubs, and task.
agent_relevance: Replications reveal task as a moderator. Test any scaffold on many tasks, not one, or the effect sign may flip.

source: Fucci et al. blind-analysis and enhanced TDD replications (search-snippet summary)
finding: Replications of an Erdogmus TDD experiment partly confirmed the original. They found no evidence that TDD improves external quality or productivity over test-last, but process conformance correlated with quality.
numbers: Baseline experiment had reported TDD productivity up 27% vs iterative test-last and 7% vs waterfall. Replications found no significant differences in tests written, productivity or external quality.
limits: Not opened: this line comes from a web search summary only.
agent_relevance: Conformance to the prescribed process may matter more than the process label. Check that the agent actually follows the scaffold.

source: Fox, Ericsson, Best (2011) Do procedures for verbal reporting of thinking have to be reactive? Meta-analysis
finding: Plain think-aloud does not change performance; asking for explanations does change it (improves it); all verbal reporting slows people down.
numbers: 94 studies, nearly 3,500 participants. Think-aloud effect size r = -0.03 (indistinguishable from zero). Explanation-style reports showed positive reactivity.
limits: Not opened; figures from a web search summary. Most studies were problem solving such as chess; transfer to language tasks is limited per later reviews.
agent_relevance: Our agent's visible reasoning trace is like a think-aloud. Prompting it to explain may change its behaviour, while a plain trace may not.

source: Double and Birney (2019) Reactivity to measures of metacognition (review)
finding: Review of whether measuring thinking changes thinking. Cites the Fox 2011 meta-analysis and the Fox and Charness 2010 study.
numbers: Fox et al. 2011: 94 studies, plain think-aloud not reactive, explanation requests reactive. Fox and Charness (2010): think-aloud raised Raven's matrices score in older adults by about 11 IQ points, not in younger adults; no effect on paired-associates, cube comparison or mental multiplication.
limits: Narrative review, no new data. No effect sizes or sample sizes for Fox and Charness on the page. Only the first 100,000 characters were read.
agent_relevance: Reactivity depends on task and population. Check whether our scaffold's logging changes agent results.

source: Ahmed, Devanbu, Treude, Pradel (2025) Can LLMs replace manual annotation of SE artifacts?
finding: Six LLMs applied to ten annotation tasks from five datasets. Agreement with humans can match human-human agreement on some tasks but not others. Model-model agreement predicts when it works.
numbers: Name-value inconsistency task: human-human Krippendorff alpha 0.52, human-model 0.49. GPT-4 kept human-level agreement when replacing up to 50% of samples on the Nalin task, saving 16.5% of total effort. For code-summary accuracy, adequacy and similarity, 100% of one rating could be replaced (33% of total effort with three ratings). Causality dataset (11 raters): 9% saving. Sesame goals: 30%.
limits: Rating tasks, 200 samples per task. Model confidence (output probability) picks which samples are safe to hand to an LLM.
agent_relevance: Use model-model agreement as a cheap test of whether a rating task is LLM-suitable before relying on LLM judges in our evaluation.

source: Liang et al. (2024) Can GPT-4 replicate empirical SE research?
finding: GPT-4 surfaces correct assumptions and sensible plans for replications but its code is mostly broken.
numbers: Seven papers, 14 SE-research participants as raters. 86% of assumptions rated partially or fully correct, relevance 3.2/5, insight 2.8/5 (only 31% insightful). 89% of analysis plans partially or fully correct, 72% of modules. Only 30% of generated code modules ran as-is.
limits: Rater panel small. GPT-4 era (2023). Code errors reflected missing SE data knowledge.
agent_relevance: LLMs are decent at methodology planning, weak at execution. Separate the plan stage from the run stage and verify code by running it.

source: Baltes et al. (2026) Guidelines for empirical studies in SE involving LLMs
finding: Community guidelines for LLM-based SE studies because reproducibility is poor.
numbers: Angermeir et al. checked 85 LLM-centric ICSE and ASE 2024 papers. Of 18 that used OpenAI models and gave artifacts, only 5 were runnable and none fully reproduced the results. Evertz et al. found at least one LLM pitfall in each of 72 papers; only 15.7% of pitfalls were discussed. Guidelines include reporting temperature and seed and using an open LLM as a baseline.
limits: Guidelines, not an experiment. Version v8, accepted manuscript.
agent_relevance: Our harness should log model version, temperature, seeds, and include an open-model arm.

source: Camporese, Massacci, Gong (2026) LLMs for qualitative analysis fail on security-specific comments
finding: Four top LLMs coding free-text comments from a human experiment did not match human annotators reliably, even on easy comments.
numbers: Nine security-relevant codes. Models: GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen3-Max. Final-prompt table (precision, recall, accuracy, last column probably chance-corrected skill): GPT-5 0.62/0.47/0.74/0.26; Claude-4 0.57/0.51/0.74/0.30; DeepSeek-V3.2 0.79/0.64/0.83/0.53; Qwen3-Max 0.74/0.73/0.86/0.61. Only code descriptions with positive examples gave gains; more prompt refinement did not help uniformly.
limits: One experiment, CS master's students' comments, nine codes. Data were only comments with near-100% human agreement. Column labels in the extracted table were not fully clear.
agent_relevance: LLM coders are assistive, not autonomous. Qualitative coding of our own trace data needs human spot checks.

source: Alshaikh et al. (2026) Prompt strategies for LLM qualitative coding of psychological safety in SE
finding: Multi-shot prompting helped one of three LLMs. Models were run ten times each to measure stability.
numbers: Claude Haiku, DeepSeek-Chat, Gemini 2.5 Flash. Multi-shot raised Cohen's kappa for Claude Haiku by +0.034 (Wilcoxon p = 0.004), not for the other two. Run-to-run SD about 0.017 or less for DeepSeek and Haiku, 0.038 for Gemini. Over-predicted 'Sharing Negative Feedback' (bias ratio up to 5.25).
limits: Small gains, ten runs per configuration, one coding scheme.
agent_relevance: Run LLM judges repeatedly and report variance. Systematic label bias persists across models.

source: Liu et al. (2026) Agreement is not quality: blind expert verification of human and LLM qualitative coding
finding: Agreement with human coders is a flawed test for LLM coders. LLMs agreed less with humans than humans with each other, yet a blind expert judged both equally good.
numbers: 5 LLM systems and 3 human coders applied a 72-item codebook to 2,560 messages. Human-LLM Jaccard 0.30 vs human-human 0.52. Blind expert judged 855 comparisons: 51.5% preferred human, 48.5% LLM (p = 0.537). Two LLMs ranked above two of three humans in a Bradley-Terry ranking.
limits: One domain (K-12 educator messages), one expert verifier.
agent_relevance: Add blind verification of disputed items rather than relying on agreement alone when we judge our agent's outputs.

source: Kirsten et al. (2024) Decoding complexity: human-AI concordance in qualitative coding
finding: LLM-human agreement drops as coding tasks get more complex. Humans also agree less on complex tasks.
numbers: Three coding tasks of rising complexity. Humans: almost perfect agreement on two, substantial on the third. GPT-4 almost perfect on Task A, moderate on Task C; GPT-3.5 fair on Task C with one or few examples. Three examples raised GPT-3.5 on Task A from substantial to almost perfect.
limits: Short workshop paper, preliminary, one dataset.
agent_relevance: Task complexity moderates LLM coder quality. Evaluate per task, not as a blanket claim.

source: METR RCT: forecast gap (developers and experts overestimate speedup)
finding: Experts in machine learning and economics, who got the study design, also predicted a large speedup that did not appear.
numbers: Developers forecast 24% time reduction before, estimated 20% after, measured +19% time. Expert forecasters were paid up to $50 (some up to $100) per forecast and also substantially overestimated the speedup.
limits: Expert numbers by group are in the paper appendix, not read here.
agent_relevance: Expert and self-judgement of benefit is unreliable. Use measured outcomes in agent evaluation.

source: Ahmed et al. (2025): confidence and model-model agreement as selectors
finding: Samples with higher GPT-4 output probability were more likely to match the majority human label. Model-model agreement tracked human-model agreement across tasks.
numbers: Replacing random samples with the highest-confidence ones kept inter-rater agreement better than random replacement, up to about 50% for the Nalin set and 60% for the causality set. At 100% replacement agreement fell.
limits: Based on token probabilities, which closed models may not expose. Ten tasks only.
agent_relevance: Route low-confidence items to humans. Use two models disagreeing as a flag.

source: Peng et al. (2023): heterogeneity of the Copilot effect
finding: Effect varied by developer type. Authors suggest AI pair programmers may widen access to the profession.
numbers: Heterogeneous-effects regression (Horvitz-Thomson transformed outcome) on years of professional coding, daily hours coding, age and other covariates. Less experienced, heavy-load and age 25-44 developers benefited more. Control group had outliers above 300 minutes; results held when dropped.
limits: Linear-effect assumption, small sample of 95.
agent_relevance: Expect the benefit of a scaffold to be larger for weaker base models than for strong ones.

source: Liang et al. (2024): where GPT-4 failed in replication code
finding: Code from GPT-4 had correct high-level logic but many small implementation errors. Assumptions rarely applied common knowledge about SE data.
numbers: Only 30% of code modules executed as-is. 31% of assumptions were rated insightful. 86% of the 14 raters reported using LLMs.
limits: Small rater panel; GPT-4 (2023).
agent_relevance: Execution checks before trusting agent-generated analysis. Add a step where the agent runs its own code.

source: Camporese et al. (2026): prompt refinement as a moderator
finding: Richer prompts (emerging codes, codebook with examples, conflicting examples) gave one early gain, then no uniform improvement. Models over-flagged on keywords.
numbers: Gain appeared when formal code definitions with positive examples were added. Later refinements changed results little and token cost rose. DeepSeek-V3.2 and Qwen3-Max came close to human agreement; GPT-5 and Claude-4 had very low performance on some codes.
limits: Single dataset; significance not reached across codes or models.
agent_relevance: More prompt effort has diminishing returns for judging tasks. Budget tokens for a clear rubric with examples, then stop.
